stem: A prospective customer will not sign until it receives credible assurance about your security controls. Which is most appropriate to provide?

options.text: An independent third-party audit report
options.why: External parties need assurance that does not depend on your own word. Independence is what gives the report weight outside the organisation.

options.text: A completed internal self-assessment
options.why: A self-assessment is the team assessing its own controls. It is useful internally and carries no weight with a customer.

options.text: An internal audit report from your audit function
options.why: Better, and it is still the organisation auditing itself. Customers normally require genuine third-party independence.

options.text: A copy of your information security policy
options.why: A policy states intent. It is no evidence that the controls actually operate.

stem: A regulator conducts a mandatory review of a bank's security controls and issues formal findings. What is this?

options.text: A regulatory examination
options.why: A review performed by the regulator itself, which the organisation cannot decline, is an examination.

options.text: An independent third-party audit
options.why: A third-party audit is commissioned by the organisation from an audit firm. A regulator arrives on its own authority.

options.text: An internal audit
options.why: Internal audit is staffed by the organisation and reports to its audit committee.

options.text: An attestation
options.why: An attestation is a signed statement that something is true, not a review process.

stem: A penetration tester is engaged to simulate an external attacker and is given only the company name. Which type of engagement is this?

options.text: Unknown environment testing
options.why: The tester receives no internal information and must discover everything, which is the modern term for a black box test.

options.text: Partially known environment testing
options.why: That would mean the tester is given some information, such as network ranges or a standard user account.

options.text: Known environment testing
options.why: Known environment testing supplies full information, including architecture diagrams, credentials and sometimes source code.

options.text: Passive reconnaissance
options.why: That describes a technique the tester will use, not how much they were told. The two are separate axes.

stem: During the opening phase of an engagement the tester reviews WHOIS records, employee LinkedIn profiles and certificate transparency logs, without sending any traffic to the target. What is this?

options.text: Passive reconnaissance
options.why: Information is gathered from third-party sources, so the target has no way to observe it.

options.text: Active reconnaissance
options.why: Active reconnaissance interacts with the target directly, such as port scanning or banner grabbing, and is visible in the target's logs.

options.text: Unknown environment testing
options.why: That describes how much the tester was told at the outset, not the technique being used now.

options.text: A vulnerability scan
options.why: A scan sends probes to the target, making it very much active.

stem: A review of a firm's controls is being redesigned so that its results carry more independence, using the same checklist. Which change adds the most?

options.text: Have a party outside the organisation perform the review
options.why: Independence is about who performs the review. An outside party is independent of both the team and the organisation.

options.text: Have the control owners repeat their self-assessment more carefully
options.why: Care does not add independence. The same people are still marking their own work.

options.text: Have the head of the audited team sign the results
options.why: A signature adds accountability, not independence. The reviewed party is still vouching for itself.

options.text: Extend the checklist with more detailed questions
options.why: Independence is about who performs the review, not which checklist they hold.

stem: A tester runs a port scan against the target's public range during the first week of an engagement. How is this classified?

options.text: Active reconnaissance
options.why: Scanning sends packets to the target and appears in its logs. Interacting with the target is what makes reconnaissance active.

options.text: Passive reconnaissance
options.why: Passive means gathering from third-party sources without touching the target: WHOIS, OSINT, certificate transparency.

options.text: Unknown environment testing
options.why: That describes how much the tester was told at the outset, not what they are doing now. The two are separate axes.

options.text: A vulnerability assessment rather than reconnaissance
options.why: A scan during reconnaissance is still reconnaissance. The phase is defined by purpose, and it is active either way.

stem: An exercise runs an attacking team and a defending team at the same time, with a third group coordinating both and feeding lessons back live. What is this called?

options.text: An integrated exercise
options.why: Offensive and defensive running together with coordination between them is the integrated form, sometimes called purple teaming.

options.text: An offensive test
options.why: Offensive describes the attacking side alone, with no defensive participation by design.

options.text: A defensive test
options.why: Defensive describes the blue team's side alone.

options.text: A tabletop exercise
options.why: A tabletop is a discussion in a room. This exercise involves teams actually operating.

stem: Before a penetration test begins, which document states what the tester may and may not touch, the hours they may test, and who to contact if something breaks?

options.text: The rules of engagement
options.why: Scope boundaries, permitted windows, prohibited techniques and escalation contacts are exactly what the rules of engagement fix before testing starts.

options.text: The statement of work
options.why: The SOW defines deliverables, timeline and price. It is commercial rather than operational.

options.text: The right-to-audit clause
options.why: That is a contractual right to inspect a vendor. It does not scope a test of your own estate.

options.text: The non-disclosure agreement
options.why: An NDA governs what the tester may say afterwards, not what they may do.

stem: A supplier provides a signed statement from its chief information security officer confirming that stated controls operated throughout the year. How much assurance does this carry compared with an independent audit?

options.text: Less: attestation attaches personal accountability to a claim, but the claim is still the organisation's own and nobody independent tested it
options.why: A signature raises the stakes for the signer and does not introduce independence. It sits above a self-assessment and below an independent audit.

options.text: More, because a named officer is personally liable
options.why: Accountability strengthens the claim without verifying it. Independent testing is what verification means.

options.text: The same, since both result in a formal statement
options.why: The output format is similar; who performed the work is not.

options.text: None, since any statement from the supplier is worthless
options.why: Overcorrection. An attestation is meaningful evidence and is weaker than independent assurance.

stem: Why does an audit committee typically sit at board level and receive internal audit reports directly rather than through management?

options.text: So that internal audit can report findings about management without those findings passing through the people they concern
options.why: Independence of the reporting line is what makes internal audit credible. Routing findings through management lets the subject of a finding edit it.

options.text: Because board members have more technical expertise than management
options.why: Usually the reverse. The committee provides independence and governance, not technical depth.

options.text: Because regulators require all audit findings to be published
options.why: Internal audit findings are generally not published, and the committee's purpose is oversight rather than disclosure.

options.text: To allow the committee to perform the audits itself
options.why: The committee oversees and directs the function; it does not carry out the work.

stem: What distinguishes an external assessment from an external audit?

options.text: An audit formally tests compliance against a defined standard and issues an opinion; an assessment evaluates posture more broadly and advises, without certifying
options.why: Audits produce an opinion against a specified standard with defined evidence. Assessments can be wider in scope and more useful for improvement, and they certify nothing.

options.text: An assessment is performed by regulators and an audit by consultants
options.why: Either can be performed by either. The distinction is the nature of the work and its output.

options.text: An audit is advisory and an assessment is binding
options.why: Reversed: the audit opinion is the formal output that others rely on.

options.text: They are the same, differing only in who commissions them
options.why: They are kept distinct because the output and the level of formality differ.

stem: Rank these from weakest to strongest assurance: external audit, self-assessment, attestation by a named officer, internal audit.

options.text: Self-assessment, attestation, internal audit, external audit
options.why: Each step adds either accountability or independence. Self-assessment has neither, attestation adds a signature, internal audit adds an independent function inside the organisation, external audit adds independence from it entirely.

options.text: External audit, internal audit, attestation, self-assessment
options.why: Reversed. Independence strengthens assurance.

options.text: Attestation, self-assessment, external audit, internal audit
options.why: An attestation is stronger than an unsigned self-assessment, and external audit is the strongest of the four.

options.text: Internal audit, self-assessment, attestation, external audit
options.why: Internal audit is stronger than both a self-assessment and an attestation, not weaker.

stem: Which TWO statements about audits and assessments are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: An audit committee exists so internal audit can report without findings passing through the management they concern
options.why: The reporting line is what preserves independence.

options.text: An attestation adds accountability to a claim but does not add independence
options.why: A signature raises the stakes for the signer; verification requires someone with no stake.

options.text: An external assessment issues a formal compliance opinion
options.why: That is an audit. Assessments evaluate and advise without certifying.

options.text: A self-assessment carries the same weight as an internal audit
options.why: Internal audit is an independent function inside the organisation; a self-assessment is the team grading itself.

options.text: Internal audit reports to the chief information security officer to preserve independence
options.why: Reporting to the function it audits is precisely what destroys independence.

stem: A bank receives notice of a regulatory examination. The CISO suggests handing the examiners the clean report from last quarter's independent third-party audit instead of giving them access to systems and staff. How should the board respond?

options.text: Accept: an independent third-party audit is stronger than a regulatory examination
options.why: Independence is not the same as authority. A regulatory examination is mandatory and carries legal consequences no private audit has.

options.text: Accept, but ask the audit firm to attest to the examiners on the bank's behalf
options.why: An attestation can support a position, yet it does not turn the regulator's examination into something the bank can delegate.

options.text: Decline: a regulatory examination is performed by the regulator on its own terms, and an independent audit report does not replace it
options.why: The regulator decides scope, access and findings. Another party's audit can be evidence in it, but it cannot stand in for the examination.

options.text: Decline, and run an internal self-assessment so the bank controls what the examiners see
options.why: A self-assessment is the weakest form of assurance and cannot limit what a regulator may examine.

stem: A physical penetration tester is stopped by a guard in a restricted corridor after tailgating through a badge door. Which document should the tester be carrying to resolve this safely?

options.text: A signed authorization that names the tester, the scope and an emergency contact, issued under the rules of engagement
options.why: Physical testers carry written permission from someone with the authority to grant it. It protects the tester and tells the guard who to call.

options.text: A verbal approval recorded by the facilities supervisor
options.why: Verbal approval from someone without authority to grant it is the situation that gets testers arrested. Authorization must be written and from an accountable owner.

options.text: The vendor's standard master service agreement
options.why: An MSA sets commercial terms. It does not name the tester, the scope or a contact for a live incident.

options.text: A copy of the company's acceptable use policy
options.why: The acceptable use policy governs employees. It gives a tester no authority at all.

stem: A penetration testing exercise is described as defensive. Which activity does that describe?

options.text: Simulating an attacker's techniques to break into systems
options.why: That is offensive testing, the red team side.

options.text: Hardening and monitoring systems, detecting simulated attacks and responding to them
options.why: Defensive covers the blue team side: prevention, detection and response against the attack being simulated.

options.text: Giving the tester architecture diagrams and credentials before testing starts
options.why: That describes how much the tester was told, which is the known, partially known and unknown axis, not offensive or defensive.

options.text: Collecting WHOIS and DNS data without contacting the target
options.why: That is passive reconnaissance, a technique, not a team role.

stem: A retailer wants to know what an attacker could do after phishing a single standard user account. The tester is given that user's credentials and the company name, and nothing else. Which type of engagement is this?

options.text: Unknown environment
options.why: Unknown means the tester starts with nothing beyond a target. A supplied credential is inside knowledge.

options.text: Known environment
options.why: Known means broad disclosure, such as diagrams, configurations and often source. One credential is far short of that.

options.text: Passive reconnaissance
options.why: Passive and active describe whether the target can see the tester. They do not say how much the tester was told.

options.text: Partially known environment
options.why: Some knowledge, here one low-privilege credential, is given and the rest must be found. That is partially known.

stem: A tester reads the target's job postings, searches a public index of exposed services and reviews archived copies of its website. Which next step is the first one the target's own logs could record?

options.text: Searching certificate transparency logs for the target's domains
options.why: Certificate transparency logs are a public third party record, so the target never sees the query.

options.text: Running a TCP port scan against the target's public range
options.why: Everything before the scan was gathered from third parties. The scan sends packets to the target, so it is the first active step and the first the target could see.

options.text: Reading cached banner data from an internet scanning service
options.why: The scanning service touched the target, not the tester. Reading its archive is still passive.

options.text: Reviewing the staff directory published on a professional networking site
options.why: This is open source gathering from a third party. The target is not contacted.

stem: Three months before a certification audit, a company wants an honest view of whether its controls meet the standard, using its own staff and without involving the certifier. What should it run?

options.text: An internal compliance audit against the standard's requirements
options.why: Internal audit tests the organization's own controls against a standard or policy, which is the usual way to prepare before an external auditor arrives.

options.text: A regulatory examination
options.why: A regulatory examination is carried out by a regulator. An organization cannot schedule one for itself.

options.text: An attestation signed by the CISO
options.why: An attestation is a statement that controls operate. It does not test whether they do.

options.text: An independent third-party audit by the certifier
options.why: The stem says to use its own staff and keep the certifier out, which is internal audit.

stem: A cloud provider selling to government wants to prove it meets a published control framework and also learn whether an outside attacker could actually get in. Which TWO activities together meet both goals? (Choose two.)

options.text: A self-assessment completed by the security team
options.why: A self-assessment has no independence and will not satisfy a government customer.

options.text: An independent third-party audit against the framework
options.why: An independent audit gives credible, outside assurance of compliance that government customers will accept.

options.text: Passive reconnaissance against its own domains only
options.why: Passive reconnaissance is a technique inside a test. On its own it shows exposure, not exploitability.

options.text: An unknown environment penetration test of its public services
options.why: An unknown environment test simulates an outside attacker and shows what is really exploitable, which an audit does not.

options.text: A written attestation from the head of engineering
options.why: An attestation is a statement, not an audit of the controls or a test of the perimeter.

stem: Which THREE statements about an unknown environment penetration test are correct? (Choose three.)

options.text: The tester starts with little more than the target's name, as an outside attacker would
options.why: That is the defining condition of an unknown environment test.

options.text: The tester is given network diagrams and administrator credentials
options.why: That is a known environment test.

options.text: Reconnaissance and discovery take up a large share of the effort
options.why: Without disclosed information, mapping the target is the tester's job, so it takes time.

options.text: It is the same thing as passive reconnaissance
options.why: Unknown describes what the tester was told. Passive describes whether the target can see the tester. A tester in an unknown environment test will also scan actively.

options.text: For the same depth of testing it usually takes longer than a known environment test
options.why: Known environment testing skips discovery. Unknown does not, so it usually costs more time for the same coverage.

stem: A hospital wants to know whether a stranger could walk into a waiting room, plug a small device into a wall network jack and whether staff would challenge them. Which type of test fits?

options.text: An internal compliance audit
options.why: An audit checks controls against a standard. It does not attempt to get through them.

options.text: A self-assessment
options.why: A self-assessment is staff scoring their own controls. It does not test anything.

options.text: A physical penetration test
options.why: The objective is to defeat physical and procedural barriers, including whether people challenge strangers. That is a physical test.

options.text: Passive reconnaissance
options.why: Passive reconnaissance never touches the target. This scenario depends on actually entering the building.

stem: A mature SOC has been through several red team exercises where it was never told what the testers were doing, and it keeps missing the same techniques. What is the main reason to move to an integrated exercise next?

options.text: It gives the testers more knowledge of the environment
options.why: How much the testers know is the known, partially known and unknown axis. Integration is about how the two sides work together.

options.text: Defenders see each technique as it is used and can tune detection immediately while testing continues
options.why: Integrated testing joins the offensive and defensive sides so lessons are applied during the exercise, rather than in a report afterwards.

options.text: It replaces the need for any defensive role
options.why: Integrated testing needs both sides working together. It removes the separation between them.

options.text: It makes the result valid as independent assurance for customers
options.why: A cooperative exercise is useful for improving detection. It is not an independent audit and does not replace one.

stem: As part of an authorized test, a tester phones the target's help desk, claims to be a new starter and asks which remote access software staff use. How should this reconnaissance be classified?

options.text: Passive, because no system was scanned
options.why: Passive means the target cannot see the tester. A phone call to the help desk is seen by the target.

options.text: Passive, because the information could be found publicly
options.why: The test is how it was collected, not whether the information is public. This was collected by asking the target.

options.text: Neither, because it is social engineering rather than reconnaissance
options.why: The information gathered is reconnaissance, and the method of interacting with the target makes it active.

options.text: Active, because it involves direct interaction with the target's people
options.why: Anything that directly engages the target, including people, is active reconnaissance, even without touching a system.

stem: Internal audit reports to the CFO, and the finance systems are among those it audits. Last year two critical findings in finance were softened before the report was issued. Which change best restores the independence of internal audit?

options.text: Have internal audit report functionally to the audit committee of the board, not to an executive it audits
options.why: Independence depends on the reporting line. Reporting to the audit committee takes the audited management out of the path of the findings.

options.text: Move internal audit under the CIO instead of the CFO
options.why: Another executive whose systems are also audited has the same conflict. The fix is reporting to the board committee.

options.text: Replace internal audit with a self-assessment by finance
options.why: A self-assessment by the audited team removes independence altogether.

options.text: Ask the CFO to sign an attestation that findings were reported in full
options.why: An attestation from the person with the conflict does not remove the conflict.

stem: A prospective customer sends a 200 question form about the company's security controls. Staff answer it from their own knowledge and records. What is this exercise?

options.text: An independent third-party audit
options.why: Nobody independent examines the evidence, so this is not an audit.

options.text: A regulatory examination
options.why: A regulator did not initiate this, and a customer form has no regulatory standing.

options.text: A self-assessment
options.why: The organization is judging its own controls. It is useful for transparency but carries little independent weight.

options.text: A defensive penetration test
options.why: Nothing is attacked or defended. It is a written questionnaire.

stem: A customer receives a cloud provider's independent audit report and wants to rely on it as assurance. Which check matters most before relying on it?

options.text: That its scope and period cover the services and dates the customer actually uses
options.why: An independent report only assures what it examined. If the scope leaves out the services in use, or the period has lapsed, it says little about the customer's own exposure.

options.text: That the provider's own internal audit team produced it
options.why: Internal production is the opposite of what makes the report independent.

options.text: That it comes with a signed CEO attestation in place of audit findings
options.why: An attestation is a statement. It does not replace findings examined by an independent party.

options.text: That it lists no exceptions at all, since any exception makes it unusable
options.why: Exceptions are normal. What matters is whether any of them touch the services the customer relies on.

stem: A tester reads the target's job postings, public DNS records and social media without sending any traffic to its systems. Which kind of reconnaissance is this?

options.text: Passive reconnaissance
options.why: Gathering from public sources without interacting with the target is passive.

options.text: Active reconnaissance
options.why: Active reconnaissance touches the target's systems directly. Nothing here does.

options.text: Integrated testing
options.why: Integrated testing joins offensive and defensive work. It says nothing about how information was gathered.

options.text: Defensive testing
options.why: Defensive testing is the defenders' side of an exercise, not a way of collecting information.

stem: A tester runs a port scan against the target's whole address range. Which kind of reconnaissance is this?

options.text: Passive reconnaissance
options.why: Passive work never sends traffic to the target. A scan does.

options.text: Active reconnaissance
options.why: Probing the target's systems directly, as a scan does, is active, and it can be noticed.

options.text: Offensive testing only
options.why: Offensive describes the attacking side. Active and passive describe how information is gathered.

options.text: Physical testing
options.why: Physical testing is about buildings and people. A port scan is a network activity.

stem: A penetration test brings the attackers and the defenders together, so the two sides work as one team and lessons pass between them throughout. What is this called?

options.text: Offensive penetration testing
options.why: Offensive is the attacking side alone.

options.text: Defensive penetration testing
options.why: Defensive is the defending side alone.

options.text: Integrated penetration testing
options.why: Integrated testing combines the offensive and defensive sides into one approach.

options.text: Passive reconnaissance
options.why: That is a way of gathering information, not a team arrangement.

stem: In a penetration test exercise, which team tries to detect and block the testers' activity?

options.text: The offensive team
options.why: The offensive team is the one doing the attacking.

options.text: The attestation team
options.why: Attestation is a statement that controls are in place. It is not a role in a test.

options.text: The audit committee
options.why: An audit committee oversees audit reports at board level. It does not sit in the exercise.

options.text: The defensive team
options.why: The defenders watch for and respond to the attack. That is the defensive role.
